issues.issue: The preamble treats "Fund" and "Plan" as interchangeable labels for the same thing, whereas operative Sections 1.20 and 1.22 give "Plan" (the benefit rules) and "Trust Fund" (the assets) distinct meanings. A dispute over which body of terms governs could turn on that recital-versus-definition mismatch.

The recital says the Collective Bargaining Agreements "establish the Plan," but operative Section 1.20 defines the Plan as rules "from time to time adopted by the Board" and Section 4.2 vests amendment of the Plan in the Board. A party arguing the CBA fixes plan terms would rely on the recital against the operative text.

The recital limits the Trust to the "exclusive purpose of providing pension and retirement benefits," while operative Section 2.2 and Section 5.3 also authorise financing the operation and administration of the Trust and paying its expenses. The recital and the operative expense provisions point in different directions on what the corpus may be spent on.

The recital rests the amendment power on "Paragraph 18 of the Trust Agreement," a paragraph number that exists nowhere in the restated instrument, whose amendment provision is Section 10.1. That dangling cross-reference leaves the asserted authority unverifiable on the face of the document.

Section 1.1 lets the "Administrator" be the Board itself or a delegate, while Section 1.6 fixes the Board as the ERISA "administrator" and Section 7.1 assigns distinct duties to an Administrator. Which entity bears an Administrator duty in a given case is left uncertain across those provisions.

The definition names the "Publishers' Association of New York," whereas the preamble and the signature block identify the party as the Publishers' Association of New York City. The dropped word makes the defined party's identity turn on a scrivener's slip.

"Both the Chairman and Secretary of the Board" is ambiguous as to whether an Authorized Person means the two officers acting jointly or each of them individually. The rest of the definition, which lists single individuals in the alternative, does not resolve it.

"Internal Revenue Code of 1936" is a mechanical error; there is no such Code, and the instrument elsewhere invokes Sections 401(a), 501(a) and 4975, which are provisions of the 1986 Code. The mistake makes the defined term literally refer to a non-existent statute.

A writing counts as a "Collective Bargaining Agreement" only if it "is acceptable to the Board," a standard with no criteria and no procedure for acceptance. Whether a given participation agreement qualifies is therefore left to an unbounded judgment.

The definition incorporates the Collective Trust's own agreement by reference "to the extent not inconsistent with the terms of this Agreement," while simultaneously giving that trust's trustees "sole and exclusive authority" over transferred assets in tension with Section 5.7's diversification and prudence duty. Which document governs a transferred asset is left to be worked out.

Section 1.10 requires only "at least one Employer Trustee and one Union Trustee," while Section 5.6(b) requires two or more Trustees in equal numbers from each side. The two composition rules for the same body are stated differently.

The definition invokes "Corporate Trustee" "as that term is defined in Section 3.12," but Section 3.12 contains no definition — it only authorises the Board to appoint a bank or trust company as one. The cross-reference points to a definition that does not exist.

An Employer Trustee is defined solely as one "designated pursuant to Section 3.3(a)," which names two specific individuals, yet successors are designated under Section 3.9 by certificate of the Association. On the literal definition a Section 3.9 successor is not an Employer Trustee.

The definition requires Instructions to be "written communications signed by an Authorized Person," then expressly includes telex and similar transmissions that carry no signature and are validated only by a "reasonable degree of certainty" as to the sender. The signature requirement and the included examples cannot both be applied literally.

The definition makes it a condition of being an Investment Manager that the appointee "has acknowledged in writing to the Board" its fiduciary status, whereas Section 8.3 makes obtaining that acknowledgment optional ("The Board may require"). An appointee without a certificate is simultaneously an Investment Manager under Article 8 and not one under Section 1.18.

Section 1.20 defines "Plan" as the Board's benefit rules, but the Preamble uses "Plan" as an alternative name for the Fund itself. The same defined term carries two different referents in the instrument.

The definition is an enumerated list of eleven categories introduced by "including, but not limited to" and closed by catch-all (k), so the reach of the general words against the specific enumeration is open. Whether an instrument outside the list is a "Security" is left to ejusdem generis argument.

Section 1.22 sweeps in all property deposited in the trust account or held by a Custodian, while Section 5.5(w) directs that contributions collected for another plan be segregated and "shall not be deemed plan assets of the Fund." Whether segregated monies are Trust Fund assets depends on which provision controls.

"And any affiliates thereof" is undefined and sets no test for affiliation, so the set of labour organisations whose agreements bind the Fund has no stated boundary. Whether a particular local is within the "Union" cannot be answered from the text.

A Union Trustee is defined as one designated under Section 3.3(b), which names three individuals, but Section 3.8 provides that the Union Trustees "shall be the incumbent president, vice president and secretary-treasurer of the Union." If a named individual leaves office the two provisions identify different people as Union Trustees.

"Certain pension and related benefits" leaves the class of permissible "related" benefits undefined, and Section 4.1(a) compounds it by allowing whatever "related benefits as the Board may from time to time determine." The exclusive-purpose limit has no ascertainable boundary.

Section 2.3 provides that the Agreement "shall be deemed amended" automatically wherever it is inconsistent with the Code or ERISA, whereas Section 10.1 permits amendment only by unanimous vote of the Board subject to stated conditions. A self-executing amendment mechanism cannot be squared with the exclusive amendment procedure.

Section 2.4 makes participation depend on the employer being "acceptable to the Trustees," while Section 1.13 defines an Employer as any employer required to contribute under a Collective Bargaining Agreement with the Union, without any acceptance requirement. Whether an unaccepted signatory is bound to contribute turns on which provision governs.

The Employer is "deemed" to have "agreed to be bound unconditionally" to the Plan, the Trust and "all of the decisions of the Trustees," a deemed consent whose scope — including future amendments and future decisions — is left open. The word "unconditionally" would have to be construed against the limits the Employer actually accepted by signing a CBA.

Section 3.1 fixes an unequal board of two Employer and three Union Trustees, which sits awkwardly with Section 6.3's quorum of two from each side and with Section 10.1(c)'s premise of equal voting power, and it is flatly displaced by Amendment No. 4's two-and-two composition. Which composition governs at a given date is a live question on the face of the document.

The three named Union Trustees are fixed by name, while Section 3.8 provides that the Union Trustees "shall be the incumbent president, vice president and secretary-treasurer of the Union." The two provisions identify Union Trustees by different criteria and can diverge the moment an officer changes.

Section 3.1 states that "the appointment of Trustees shall be governed by the provisions of Section 3.4," but Section 3.4 prescribes no appointment mechanism at all — it only requires that copies of appointments be filed and acceptances signed. The referenced governing provision is empty of the substance it is said to supply.

Section 3.6 requires notice to "the Contributing Employer that designated him as a Trustee" and deems a Trustee resigned when "the Contributing Employer which designated him" ceases contributing, yet under Sections 3.1, 3.3, 3.7 and 3.9 Employer Trustees are designated by the Association and Union Trustees by the Union — no Contributing Employer designates anyone. The automatic-resignation trigger cannot be applied to any Trustee actually appointed under this instrument.

The section is headed "Removal of Union Trustees" but contains no removal power at all; it prescribes who the Union Trustees shall be and addresses only removal "by operation of law." Whether the Union may remove its Trustees, and by what means, is unanswerable from the provision that purports to govern it.

Section 3.8 makes the Union Trustees the incumbent president, vice president and secretary-treasurer ex officio, while Section 3.1 says they are "selected by the Union" and Section 3.3(b) names three individuals. The three provisions supply three different rules for who holds the office.

The sentence says the principal officer "shall designate a successor Union Trustee by filing... a certification," then adds "in which case a Successor Union Trustee shall be elected from the full-time officers of the Union." Designation by one officer and election from among the officers are two different mechanisms and the provision commands both.

Section 1.12 treats "Corporate Trustee" as a term "defined in Section 3.12," but 3.12(a) only confers a power of appointment and defines nothing. The definitional chain between the two provisions is broken.

The delegation closes with "such other duties and powers as the Board may deem advisable" after two specific grants, leaving the reach of the general words against the enumerated specifics open. Whether non-investment fiduciary functions can be handed to the Corporate Trustee turns on that catch-all.

Allowing the Corporate Trustee to hold the Fund "as sole trustee of a trust separate from the Fund created by this Trust Agreement" is hard to reconcile with Section 1.22, which defines the Trust Fund to include property held by a Custodian, and with Section 7.2's allocation of overall responsibility to the Board. Whether assets so held remain Trust Fund assets is left unresolved.

The clause releases the Trustees "forever" from "any responsibility or liability" for transferred assets, while Section 5.9 opens "Except as may otherwise be provided by ERISA" and Section 5.7 imposes a continuing prudence and diversification duty on the Board. The unqualified release cannot be squared with those provisions.

The limitation permits "no benefits other than pension, retirement, and such other related benefits as the Board may from time to time determine," so the general words at the end dissolve the very restriction the specifics create. What falls outside the enumerated categories is a matter the Board defines for itself.
